title: The Little Ships of Dunkirk
text:
In late May 1940 the German advance had trapped the British Expeditionary Force and many French troops against the coast at Dunkirk. The Admiralty launched Operation Dynamo to bring them home across the Channel. The problem was that the beaches shelved gently, and big ships could not get close enough to take men off.

The call went out for small craft. Pleasure cruisers, fishing boats, lifeboats, ferries, barges and private motor yachts were gathered from the Thames and the south coast ports. Many were crewed by naval reservists, others by their own owners and fishermen who refused to hand them over. They crossed under air attack, ran in to the beaches, and ferried soldiers out to the destroyers and transports waiting offshore, trip after trip.

Hundreds of these little ships took part, and a good number were sunk or wrecked. Most of the troops actually left from the harbor's long stone mole aboard destroyers and larger vessels, but the small boats made the beach evacuation possible and carried many thousands themselves.

When the operation ended on 4 June, about 338,000 Allied soldiers had been brought to England, far more than the few tens of thousands planners had hoped for. Churchill warned Parliament that "wars are not won by evacuations." But the army that would fight on had been saved, by a navy working alongside a flotilla of civilians.
lesson: Large institutions often succeed only when ordinary people step in with what they have. A big effort can be made of many small, willing contributions.
people: Bertram Ramsay, civilian boat owners and crews, Royal Navy
location: Dunkirk, France, and the English Channel
source: Walter Lord, The Miracle of Dunkirk (1982); Winston Churchill, speech to the House of Commons, 4 June 1940
caveat: Popular memory overstates the little ships' share: most soldiers were lifted from the harbor mole by destroyers and larger ships.
